note: Track sevenths-up, step 8: 9th chords, the 9 stacked on a 7th chord, tapped on the staff, compared with the 7th chord on the chord circle and checked in the ear game ("qualities": 7 and 9, its answers named as the buttons show them), then heard coming in over a backing track. The key is moves (any key): the old Key selector is gone, the staff, circle and backing track follow the key, the chord is named as {{=key}}, and a {{?key}} line says what stays the same.

exercise.title: 9th chords: a 7th chord with the 9
exercise.why: A 9th chord is a 7th chord with the 2nd above its root added an octave up, so hearing that one high note come and go tells a 9 from a 7.

cells.text:
{{=key}}9 is {{=key}}7 with one more note stacked on top. Tap {{1}}, {{3}}, {{5}} and {{b7}} from the low {{1}} on the staff below, then the ringed {{2}} above the high {{1}}: that note is the 9th.
Then tap the low {{1}} and the {{2}} next to it: the same note as the 9th, an octave lower.
Practice until you can hum the 9th before you tap it.

The circle below has the chord on {{=key}} in the middle, the 5th chord of a major key, with the chords it can turn into around it. Press {{=key}}7 on the circle, then {{=key}}9.
Then press Start in the game under it: it plays a 7th or a 9th chord from any root, and you pick Dominant 7 or Dominant 9.
Practice until you hear the high note of the 9th before you pick.

Press Play below to start the backing track: three 7th chords of a key for four bars, then the same three as 9th chords for four bars.
Look away from the chord boxes and call out "9" when the 9th chords come in.
Practice until you hear the extra note the moment the 9th chords start.
{{?key}}In another key the chords have other names, and the 9th is still the 2nd of each chord, an octave up.
